There is a particular kind of afternoon I keep returning to in memory, even though I am not sure it ever happened exactly the way I remember it. It is late summer, the light is thick and tired, and I am somewhere I should not quite be — not in any dangerous sense, only in the soft, unsupervised sense that belonged to childhood before everyone carried a glowing map in their pocket. I am on a bicycle, or perhaps on foot, on a street that looks familiar until it suddenly doesn't. The houses thin out. A dog watches me from behind a fence without barking. I have the exciting, slightly nauseating feeling that I have gone one turn too far. I am lost, but not urgently. No one knows precisely where I am, including me, and for a few minutes the world feels larger than the version of it I have been handed.

I think we have lost the art of being lost, and in losing it, we have lost something else quieter and more important: the ability to be surprised by our own lives.

When I was a child, I was obsessed with atlases. Not the practical kind people kept in cars, folded wrong and stuffed into glove compartments, but enormous, oversized books of the world that smelled faintly of dust and library glue. I would lie on the floor and trace coastlines with a finger, marveling at the names. Ouagadougou. Reykjavik. Tierra del Fuego. The Atacama. Places that sounded less like locations and more like incantations. I had no real desire to go to most of them, not then. What I wanted was the feeling that they existed simultaneously with my small bedroom, my school, the grocery store where my mother bought milk. That while I was brushing my teeth, wind was moving across a desert I would never see, and people were waking up to a language I would never speak, and eating breakfast foods I could not imagine. The atlas made the world feel unfinishably large. It resisted summary.

That feeling is harder to access now. Now the world arrives pre-summarized. It fits. It loads quickly. We can drop a pin, we can zoom, we can read three reviews of a waterfall before we have heard its water. We can walk through a city on a screen before our plane has landed, entering restaurants virtually, tilting the view left and right like a god with a mouse. This is miraculous, obviously. I am not romantic enough, or foolish enough, to pretend I would give up the miracle. When it rains in a strange city and you are hungry and tired, a map on a phone is mercy. But mercy and wonder are different things, and a life arranged entirely for convenience eventually begins to feel airless. We optimized away the detour, and the detour was where a lot of living happened.

I do not mean the grand, cinematic detour — quitting your job, moving to Lisbon, falling in love with a stranger on a train — though those have their place. I mean the small detours. The wrong turn that leads you past a bakery you would have never found. The closed road that forces you through a neighborhood of astonishing gardens. Getting off at the wrong bus stop and discovering that a fifteen-minute walk can reset a bad day more effectively than an hour of scrolling. These accidents were once structural features of life. Now we have to schedule them, which almost defeats the purpose. We download apps for spontaneity. We plan to wander between 2:00 and 3:30, weather permitting.

Walking, real walking without a destination optimizing your route, is a subversive act now. It says: I am not a delivery. I am not trying to minimize myself. A walk is the oldest technology we have for thinking. Darwin had a sand walk. Dickens walked London at night until the city loosened its stories. Beethoven carried manuscript paper into the woods. There is a rhythm to it that the mind falls into, a gentle rocking of thought. Ideas that refuse to arrive at a desk will sidle up to you at a crosswalk, embarrassed by their lateness. I have solved — or at least softened — more problems between the grocery store and home than I ever have staring at a screen, willing a solution to appear. The body moves, and some stubborn internal door swings open on its hinge. Maybe this is because walking reminds the brain that it lives in an animal. We spend so much of our time treating ourselves as eyes attached to thumbs. Walking restores the rest of the cast.

Cities understand this intuitively. The great ones are not efficient. Paris is a labyrinth that flirts with you. Tokyo is a puzzle that rewards respectful confusion. Istanbul, Lisbon, Mexico City, New Orleans — they all have that quality of layered time, of streets that were not planned but accumulated, like sentences revised by many hands. Even a small town can have it if you look long enough: the alley behind the pharmacy where teenagers once smoked, the bench where the same man has fed pigeons for a decade, the mural fading on a brick wall that someone painted with total sincerity and imperfect skill. A city is not its landmarks. A city is its repetitions and its secrets. You do not learn it by seeing everything. You learn it the way you learn a person: by being around long enough for it to stop performing.

That is, I suspect, why libraries still feel holy to so many of us, even those of us who are not particularly nostalgic. A library is one of the last indoor places where you are not expected to buy anything, prove anything, or be anyone in particular. You can be broke, curious, lonely, studious, homeless, brilliant, bored, a new parent with a stroller, an old man doing the crossword in pen — the library takes all comers. And crucially, its shelves still allow for browsing, that endangered art. An algorithm can recommend you a book based on other books you have liked, and it will often be correct, and correctness can become a prison. Browsing is different. Browsing is running your eyes across a shelf of books about geology when you came in for a novel, and pulling one out because its spine is a beautiful shade of green, and opening it to a photograph of a glacier that makes you feel, suddenly and inexplicably, sad about time. No algorithm would have predicted the glacier. The glacier was not for you, which is precisely why it found you.

The internet promised us an infinite library, and in many ways it delivered. I can learn about glacier formation, or bread baking, or medieval siege weapons, or the mating habits of octopuses at 2 a.m. in my kitchen, and that is a wonder my atlas-loving childhood self would have traded years to possess. But the infinite library has a problem the physical one doesn't: it knows you're there, and it wants things from you. It watches what you linger on. It learns your fears faster than your hopes. It gets very good at showing you slightly more extreme versions of what you already believe, until the world narrows into a hall of mirrors and you mistake the echo for the truth. A physical library does not rearrange its shelves at night based on your insecurities. It just stands there, patient and indifferent, which in this era feels like a form of love.

Attention is the real territory being fought over, and we all sense it. We feel it in the phantom buzz in our pockets, in the way a quiet moment instantly becomes a moment to check something, in how hard it has become to watch a sunset without photographing it, as if the unrecorded sunset might not count. I am not preaching here — I do it too, constantly, and then feel a low-grade shame about it, and then do it again. The phone is not evil. It is just very, very good at its job, and its job is not my wellbeing. Its job is to make the next thirty seconds slightly more stimulating than whatever I am currently doing, and it will win that contest against almost any ordinary moment. But ordinary moments are the substance of a life. If I trade them all away for thirty-second increments of stimulation, I will arrive at the end having been entertained continuously and having remembered almost nothing.

Because memory, it turns out, does not care much about stimulation. Memory cares about distinctiveness and emotion and story. Ask yourself what you did online three Tuesdays ago and you will get a blur. Ask yourself about the night the power went out, or the stranger who helped you change a tire in the rain, or the meal that went hilariously wrong, and the details arrive with embarrassing richness: the smell, the light, who laughed first. Our brains are not hard drives. They are storytellers with an agenda, keeping what helped us understand something, discarding the rest. This is why travel photographs so often disappoint. You stand before some vast canyon, feeling appropriately small, and you take the picture, and later the picture shows you — a canyon. Flat. Polite. The feeling is gone. The photograph kept the shape of the thing and lost the size of it, because the size of it was never in the canyon alone. It was in your tired legs, the wind, the companion who went quiet beside you, the sudden thought of your father. Context is the real photograph, and context cannot be captured, only lived.

And yet we try, endlessly, because we are terrified of forgetting. I understand the terror. I have lost people, as everyone does eventually, and discovered that memory is an unreliable friend — generous at first, then gradually thrifty. A voice you swore you'd never forget becomes, after some years, something you have to reconstruct. You remember that you loved how they laughed more than the exact sound of the laugh. This used to frighten me. Now I think it is bearable, and maybe even merciful, because it forces memory to become something other than storage. What remains of people, when the details fade, is the shape they left in you: the phrases you now say in their cadence, the standards you keep because they kept them, the way you set a table or forgive an offense or notice a bird. The dead live in our habits. That is not a small haunting. That is the main one.

Language is a habit too, and another place where getting lost pays off. I love the specific, untranslatable words other languages keep in their pockets: the Portuguese *saudade*, a longing for something absent that might never return; the Japanese *komorebi*, sunlight filtering through leaves; the German *Fernweh*, a homesickness for places you have never been. English speakers like to steal these words and pass them around, and I think we steal them because they name feelings we have had but had filed under vague weather. A good word is a window cut into a wall you didn't know was there. Suddenly the room has light. This is also what poetry does, and why people who claim not to like poetry will still weep at a funeral when the right lines are read aloud. They didn't dislike poetry. They disliked being made to feel things on a schedule, in a classroom, under fluorescent light. Poetry encountered at the right moment is not literature. It is first aid.

Names matter in a smaller way too. I have always loved learning the names of things I previously walked past in ignorance: trees, clouds, birds, stars, the parts of a shoe, the bones of the hand. An unnamed world is a blurry world. To learn that the tree outside is not just a tree but a linden, that the cloud is not just a cloud but a cumulus fractus tearing itself apart, that the bird making that liquid, fluting call is a thrush — this does not reduce the mystery. It sharpens it. It turns scenery into company. Adam's first job, in the old story, was naming, and maybe the point was not dominion but attention. You cannot love what you cannot distinguish. You cannot protect what you call, vaguely, "nature" or "stuff" or "out there." Specificity is a form of care.

We have largely outsourced our specificity. We no longer need to know which way is north, or how to read a tide table, or what phase the moon is in, though the moon continues to act on oceans and perhaps on sleep whether we consult it or not. I learned recently that boredom — true, unmedicated boredom — is becoming a rare experience, and its rarity may be costing us more than we think. Boredom is not nothing. Boredom is the mind left alone with its own unfinished business. Children who are bored invent games with sticks that become, through sheer narrative commitment, light sabers, wizard staffs, divining rods. Adults who are bored do the dishes slowly and have the thought they've been avoiding for six months. Almost every creative act I admire began as someone tolerating an empty stretch without reaching for anesthesia. The shower thought is famous precisely because the shower is one of the last places we cannot bring a screen. We have waterproofed almost everything except our own heads.

Making things with your hands is another way back. I am not skilled, and I think that matters to say. I have baked bread that could have been used in construction. I have attempted repairs that ended with a quiet trip to buy a replacement. But the attempt teaches something the successful purchase never does: respect for the made world. After you have tried to sew a straight seam, you look at a shirt differently. After you have tried to throw a pot, every mug becomes a small miracle of symmetry. After you have grown tomatoes — really grown them, fought the hornworms, cursed the blight, waited through the green weeks — a tomato is no longer a red unit from the store. It is August, in edible form. Competence is wonderful, but beginnerhood has its own sacrament. It returns you to a world where things resist you, where materials have opinions, where the wooden board splits if you are careless with the grain. Screens rarely resist us; they yield, they load, they refresh. Matter says no, and in saying no, it tells the truth.

Maybe that is why conversations with strangers remain so disproportionately memorable. A stranger has not been optimized for you. They will tell you a long story about their brother's boat when you only asked about the weather. They will hold beliefs you find baffling and kindnesses you find disarming, sometimes in the same sentence. I have been given directions, peaches, unsolicited life advice, a seat, a warning about a speed trap, and once, at a bus stop in the rain, half an umbrella and the entire plot of a soap opera I never watched. These exchanges do not scale. They cannot be monetized efficiently. They are inefficient in exactly the way friendship is inefficient, and meals are inefficient, and falling in love is the least efficient thing a person can do with their calendar. Efficiency is a fine servant for factories and a terrible master for a life. A life run like a factory produces a great deal, on time, and wonders why the warehouse feels empty.

At night, when the sky cooperates, I try to look up. Most of us live under a ceiling of light pollution now, a permanent twilight that hides all but the most stubborn stars. But drive an hour from the city — you know this, everyone who has done it knows this — and the sky remembers itself. The Milky Way is not a metaphor out there. It is a spill, a scar of light, so dense it looks like weather. I never feel properly calibrated until I have seen it. Under a real night sky, your anxieties do not disappear; they resize. That email is still embarrassing. That deadline is still real. But they take their place in a cosmos that was not arranged around your inbox, and there is relief in that demotion. We are not the main characters of the universe. We are, at best, very lucky extras who got a few speaking lines. I find this consoling beyond all reason.

I suppose what I am circling, in this long and admittedly wandering essay, is that I do not want a life that fits entirely in my hand. I want friction. I want the long way home. I want to be interrupted by beauty I didn't search for, corrected by people I didn't choose, slowed down by weather, weathered by time into someone with interesting edges. I want my days to have some unindexed hours in them — hours that produce nothing, prove nothing, and are therefore mine. I want to keep a few skills embarrassingly analog: reading a paper map badly, identifying six constellations, making soup without a recipe, writing a letter by hand with my terrible handwriting and sending it anyway, because someone receiving actual mail, with a stamp slightly crooked, feels a small and specific joy that no notification has ever replicated.

None of this requires a cabin, a sabbatical, or throwing technology into a lake, satisfying as that image briefly is. It requires something smaller and harder: choosing, a few times a day, the less optimized path. Walk the route you don't know. Leave the phone in another room while the kettle boils, and actually watch the kettle, like generations did, finding in its rising steam a tolerable place to think. Go to the library and leave with the wrong book. Learn the name of one bird. Cook the complicated thing. Call, rather than text, the friend whose voice you miss, and accept the inefficiency of a real conversation, with its pauses and overlaps and laughter that arrives late because someone was mid-sip. Sit on a bench with no agenda and watch the theater of other people's afternoons. Get a little bit lost, in a safe place, on purpose, and notice how your senses wake up when the autopilot switches off. You attend to street names. You listen. You remember how to navigate by feel and landmark and hunch, those old animal instruments, and they still work. They were never gone. They were just waiting for a signal that you needed them.

When I think back to that late-summer afternoon, the one that may not have happened exactly as I remember, what I cherish is not the being lost. It is the finding my way back. There is a specific triumph in rounding a corner and recognizing something — the water tower, the gas station with the broken sign, the oak that leans like it's listening — and feeling the map inside you click quietly into alignment with the map outside. You did that. No voice from the sky recalculated. You were confused, and then you were patient, and then you were oriented, and the neighborhood was yours in a way it had never been when you were only passing through it correctly. That sequence — confusion, patience, orientation — is basically the plot of every worthwhile thing: every craft learned, every friendship deepened, every grief survived, every self revised.

So here is my small, unfashionable hope, offered freely at the end of these pages: may we all get lost a little more, and find our way back a little slower, and pay better attention on the way. The world is still unfinishably large. It is still happening simultaneously with our small rooms. Wind is still moving across deserts we will never see, and somewhere a thrush is making its liquid call whether or not anyone has learned its name. But some of it — a street, a library shelf, a loaf, a bench, a sky — is within walking distance, waiting not to be consumed but to be noticed. All we have to do, some afternoons, is take the turn we don't recognize, and keep our eyes open until it becomes, in the best and most ordinary miracle, familiar.

None of this requires a cabin, a sabbatical, or throwing technology into a lake, satisfying as that image briefly is. It requires something smaller and harder: choosing, a few times a day, the less optimized path. Walk the route you don't know. Leave the phone in another room while the kettle boils, and actually watch the kettle, like generations did, finding in its rising steam a tolerable place to think. Go to the library and leave with the wrong book. Learn the name of one bird. Cook the complicated thing. Call, rather than text, the friend whose voice you miss, and accept the inefficiency of a real conversation, with its pauses and overlaps and laughter that arrives late because someone was mid-sip. Sit on a bench with no agenda and watch the theater of other people's afternoons. Get a little bit lost, in a safe place, on purpose, and notice how your senses wake up when the autopilot switches off. You attend to street names. You listen. You remember how to navigate by feel and landmark and hunch, those old animal instruments, and they still work. They were never gone. They were just waiting for a signal that you needed them.

When I think back to that late-summer afternoon, the one that may not have happened exactly as I remember, what I cherish is not the being lost. It is the finding my way back. There is a specific triumph in rounding a corner and recognizing something — the water tower, the gas station with the broken sign, the oak that leans like it's listening — and feeling the map inside you click quietly into alignment with the map outside. You did that. No voice from the sky recalculated. You were confused, and then you were patient, and then you were oriented, and the neighborhood was yours in a way it had never been when you were only passing through it correctly. That sequence — confusion, patience, orientation — is basically the plot of every worthwhile thing: every craft learned, every friendship deepened, every grief survived, every self revised.

So here is my small, unfashionable hope, offered freely at the end of these pages: may we all get lost a little more, and find our way back a little slower, and pay better attention on the way. The world is still unfinishably large. It is still happening simultaneously with our small rooms. Wind is still moving across deserts we will never see, and somewhere a thrush is making its liquid call whether or not anyone has learned its name. But some of it — a street, a library shelf, a loaf, a bench, a sky — is within walking distance, waiting not to be consumed but to be noticed. All we have to do, some afternoons, is take the turn we don't recognize, and keep our eyes open until it becomes, in the best and most ordinary miracle, familiar.
